---
title: "Get started with a5view"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 120
)
```

a5view draws [A5](https://a5geo.org) cells, the pentagonal cells of a
global, equal-area grid. [a5R](https://belian-earth.github.io/a5R/)
makes and works with the cells; a5view draws them in two ways:
`geom_a5()` adds them to a ggplot2 plot, and `a5_view()` puts them on an
interactive web map. Both take the same input:

- an `a5_cell` vector, or a data frame with an `a5_cell` column, one
  cell per row;
- an `a5_covering` vector, or a data frame with an `a5_covering`
  column, one set of cells per row (see [Coverings](#coverings)).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(a5view)
library(a5R)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Cells

`a5_lonlat_to_cell()` gives the cell that contains a point at a chosen
resolution. Resolution 0 has 12 cells over the globe, and each further
resolution has about four times as many; at resolution 18 a cell is
about 22 m across. `s2_santiago`, which ships with a5view, holds a
Sentinel-2 image of central Santiago, Chile, already indexed to
resolution-18 cells:

```{r data}
head(s2_santiago)
```

In ggplot2 the cells go to the `cell` aesthetic, and every other
aesthetic works as usual. Here the fill is NDVI, a vegetation index
computed from the near-infrared and red bands:

```{r ndvi}
s2_santiago$NDVI <- with(s2_santiago, (B08 - B04) / (B08 + B04))

ggplot(s2_santiago, aes(cell = cell, fill = NDVI)) +
  geom_a5() +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens", direction = 1)
```

`a5_view()` takes the same data. `fill` names a column, or an
expression of columns, as `aes()` does:

```{r ndvi-map}
a5_view(s2_santiago, fill = NDVI, opacity = 0.8)
```

Hover over a cell to see its id and value; click to pin it.

## Coverings

A *covering* is a set of cells at one resolution that stands for an
area: the cells within a radius of a point, around a cell, or inside a
polygon. a5R builds them with `a5_spherical_cap()`, `a5_grid_disk()`
and `a5_polygon_to_cells()`.

A covering is stored *compacted*: wherever all four children of a
parent cell are present, the parent is stored in their place, so a
large covering stores far fewer cells than it stands for. a5R's
[coverings article](https://belian-earth.github.io/a5R/articles/coverings.html)
covers this in detail.

Here is the area within 900 m of the centre of Parque O'Higgins, at
resolution 16 (cells about 73 m across):

```{r cap}
centre <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(-70.657, -33.4675, resolution = 16)
park <- a5_spherical_cap(centre, radius = 900)
park

# cells it stands for, and cells it stores
a5_count(park)
length(a5_covering_stored(park))
```

### Compacted or uncompacted

a5view draws what it is given. A covering is drawn as the cells it
stores, at their mixed resolutions; `a5_uncompact()` expands it to the
cells it stands for, all at resolution 16. Which to draw is your
choice: the compacted form shows how the covering is stored, the
uncompacted form the area it covers.

```{r compaction, fig.height = 4}
stored <- a5_covering_stored(park)
expanded <- a5_uncompact(park)
both <- data.frame(
  form = rep(c("compacted", "uncompacted"), c(length(stored), length(expanded))),
  cell = c(stored, expanded)
)
both$resolution <- factor(a5_get_resolution(both$cell))

ggplot(both, aes(cell = cell, fill = resolution)) +
  geom_a5(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~form) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(direction = -1)
```

The stored parents do not line up exactly with the children they stand
for: A5 cells nest in the index, not in space, so a parent's outline
overlaps its neighbours in places and leaves gaps in others. Drawn
uncompacted, the covering shows exactly the cells it holds.

The covering can go straight to `geom_a5()` or `a5_view()`, with no
data frame:

```{r cap-direct, fig.height = 4}
ggplot() +
  geom_a5(aes(cell = park), fill = "#74ac90", colour = "white")
```

```{r cap-map}
a5_view(park, border = "white")
```

And uncompacted:

```{r cap-map-uncompacted}
a5_view(a5_uncompact(park), border = "white")
```

### Coverings in a data frame

An `a5_covering` vector holds one covering per element, so it fits in a
data frame column next to the attributes of each area. a5view repeats
each row once per stored cell, so the other columns map to aesthetics
as usual. Here are three sites around the park, each with its own
radius:

```{r sites, fig.height = 4}
sites <- data.frame(
  name = c("A", "B", "C"),
  lon = c(-70.657, -70.667, -70.649),
  lat = c(-33.4675, -33.4605, -33.4745),
  radius = c(700, 400, 250)
)
centres <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(sites$lon, sites$lat, resolution = 16)
sites$area <- do.call(c, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sites)), function(i) {
  a5_spherical_cap(centres[i], radius = sites$radius[i])
}))

ggplot(sites, aes(cell = area, fill = name)) +
  geom_a5(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2)
```

On the map, colour the sites by a numeric column, and list other columns to
show on hover with `tooltip`. Hovering finds cells at every resolution
present, so a compacted covering's parents show their row too.

```{r sites-map}
a5_view(sites, fill = radius, tooltip = "name")
```

To draw each site uncompacted, expand the coverings and repeat each
row's attributes once per cell; `a5_count()` gives the number of cells
in each:

```{r sites-uncompacted, fig.height = 4}
cells <- data.frame(
  name = rep(sites$name, a5_count(sites$area)),
  cell = a5_uncompact(sites$area)
)

ggplot(cells, aes(cell = cell, fill = name)) +
  geom_a5(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2)
```

### Coverings and data

A covering is also a filter. `a5_contains()` tests cells against a
covering without expanding it, when the cells are at the covering's
resolution. Build the covering at the resolution of the data,
resolution 18 here, to select the image cells within 400 m of the park
centre:

```{r contains}
centre18 <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(-70.657, -33.4675, resolution = 18)
near <- a5_spherical_cap(centre18, radius = 400)
inside <- s2_santiago[a5_contains(near, s2_santiago$cell), ]
nrow(inside)

ggplot(inside, aes(cell = cell, fill = NDVI)) +
  geom_a5() +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens", direction = 1)
```

`a5_uncompact()` can also expand to a finer resolution than the
covering's own, for example to match coarse coverings to fine data:
`a5_uncompact(park, resolution = 18)` gives the resolution-18 cells
inside the resolution-16 covering.

## Large datasets

By default `a5_view()` sends every cell to the browser. For large
datasets, `aggregate = "mean"` or `"rep_child"` builds a level-of-detail
pyramid in which coarser cells summarise their children, and
`a5_build_pyramid()` saves one to a parquet file for
`a5_view_pyramid()`. A pyramid is built from cells at one resolution,
so uncompact a covering before aggregating it.
